query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are primarily due to its simple, homogeneous solid-solution state that promotes facile dislocation motion on multiple slip systems with a low intrinsic resistance (e.g., low Peierls barrier) and lacks effective microstructural obstacles such as precipitates or segregated grain-boundary phases. Introducing a minor precipitate-forming addition (e.g., Boron) should create grain boundary precipitates that impede dislocation movement, thus increasing hardness and strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar (or nearly equimolar) CoCrFeNiTi alloy with a single-phase, homogeneous solid-solution microstructure that exhibits multiple small slips during deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition of a precipitate-forming element (such as Boron) to induce intergranular or intragranular precipitates.
generation.conditions: Room temperature uniaxial mechanical testing (tensile or compression) at moderate strain rates that maintain the simple solid-solution state (i.e., no phase transformation), with microstructural characterization before and after deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence (or absence) of precipitates at grain boundaries that act as obstacles to dislocation motion; in the pristine state, the homogeneous matrix allows for extensive, easy slip.
generation.mechanism: In the as-cast solid-solution alloy, easy dislocation glide on multiple {110} or similar slip systems results in distributed, small slip events with limited dislocation pile-up and work hardening. A minor precipitate-forming addition is anticipated to generate intergranular nanoprecipitates that arrest dislocation motion and enhance local hardness, thereby raising the overall yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The untreated CoCrFeNiTi alloy will show low yield strength and hardness accompanied by evidence of widespread, unconstrained slip. Conversely, the alloy with the boron addition will exhibit an increase in grain boundary hardness, improved yield strength, and a change in dislocation behavior (with dislocation pinning observed near precipitates), validating the role of microstructural obstacles in strengthening.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties and deformation behavior of the unmodified, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy in its simple solid-solution state.
generation.boundary: Tests are constrained to conditions that do not induce secondary phase formation (i.e., maintained at room temperature and moderate strains) and assume that the simple solid-solution state persists during deformation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strengthening resulting from precipitate formation in CoCrFeNiTi is uncertain because the effectiveness of microstructural barriers and the kinetics of precipitate formation in this system are not well established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its pure, solid-solution state, and a second set with a controlled minor addition of Boron designed to induce grain boundary precipitates. Subject both sets to identical uniaxial tensile (or compression) tests while monitoring microstructural changes using electron microscopy and other techniques.
measurements: Hardness (macro and local, e.g., via nanoindentation)
Dislocation slip patterns and density (via electron microscopy)
Grain boundary character and precipitate distribution (via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength (or if dislocation behavior remains largely unchanged relative to the unmodified alloy), then the hypothesis that the absence of effective dislocation barriers in the solid-solution state is responsible for the low strength is falsified.

First-principles investigation of the micromechanical properties of fcc-hcp polymorphic high-entropy alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys offer a promising alternative in several high-technology applications concerning functional, safety and health aspects. Many of these new alloys compete with traditional structural materials in terms of mechanical characteristics. Understanding and controlling their properties are of the outmost importance in order to find the best single- or multiphase solutions for specific uses. Here, we employ first-principles alloy theory to address the micro-mechanical properties of five polymorphic high-entropy alloys in their face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phases. Using the calculated elastic parameters, we analyze the mechanical stability, elastic anisotropy, and reveal a strong correlation between the polycrystalline moduli and the average valence electron concentration. We investigate the ideal shear strength of two selected alloys under shear loading and show that the hcp phase possesses more than two times larger intrinsic strength than that of the fcc phase. Extracting information from noisy data: strain mapping during dynamic in situ SEM experiments

Abstract: AbstractAbstractMicromechanical testing techniques can reveal a variety of characteristics in materials that are otherwise impossible to address. However, unlike to macroscopic testing, these miniaturized experiments are more challenging to realize and analyze, as loading and boundary conditions can often not be controlled to the same extent as in standardized macroscopic tests. Hence, exploiting all possible information from such an experiment seems utmost desirable. In the present work, we utilize dynamic in situ microtensile testing of a nanocrystalline equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy in conjunction with initial feature tracking to obtain a continuous two-dimensional strain field. This enables an evaluation of true stress–strain data as well as of the Poisson’s ratio and allows to study localization of plastic deformation for the specimen. Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries.
